title: Paranormal Activity Review

content:
A good night’s sleep – a little surprising after the events at the Theatre Royal last night – we were expecting to be awake most of the night. Paranormal Activity left us with so many questions, some disturbing images and the need to keep the light on. But it was worth it!

Based loosely on the 2007 successful film, this production is a completely new story. Knowing that we were in the theatre to be scared, we delighted with the opening few minutes – the theatre grew gradually darker, our eyes became used to the gloom, and then a voice-over told us about phosphenes – the lights and patterns that we can see when we close our eyes. With booming grunge music and flickers of light in the dark, the curtain slowly rose to reveal a two-story house with some gloomy corners.

We met James and Lou, recently arrived in rainy London from Chicago and keen to start their married life together in a new place. There are hints of tension – the mother-in-law is keen to see a new addition to the family, the differences between home and abroad are something to navigate, and there are hints as to why they wanted to relocate, but they seemed like a happy couple.

The first half of the play focused on who they were – a couple who are working out how they are going to be together and contained some long passages of dialogue which took you away from the scary themes we knew were coming. They were playing with us, and before long, loud, startling noises made us jump in our seats; darker moments crept into the script, and we could feel their world starting to slip.

The second half of the play brought all the characters to the edge of their world, introducing new information that made us question what we had already seen and reevaluate what we thought we knew. There were moments of extreme tension on the stage, the audience completely silent and focused on the action, waiting for the dread we knew was coming. We are not going to reveal the outcome here – that would be wrong – but it left us with the sense of disquiet that we hoped for and a storyline that we will recall many times in the future.

James Bye (Eastenders, 2.22: A Ghost Story) leads the cast with confidence. He maintained his accent throughout, and we were impressed by his stature on stage. As we watched him descend into darkness, he communicated his emotions and built the tension; his body was wretched at times and utterly believable. Alongside him was Hannah Sinclair Robinson (The Play That Goes Wrong, The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time) as his wife, Lou. Her physicality was impressive, at times rigid with fear and at other times menacing. Her stillness was most impressive, holding herself against the chaos surrounding her. They made a great couple and were on stage throughout the show to carry the story forward.

We would also like to mention Caroline Faber, who played the mother. Initially appearing via video phone, she brought her character to life by changing small details in her facial expressions that let us know exactly what was going on. When she finally appeared on stage, she interacted with the other characters so well – changing the dynamic of the play and demonstrating her ability to scare. It is a wonderfully well-written character, and she elevated the whole production.

It was the little things in this production that made the difference. We have already mentioned the slow-moving curtain, but we also enjoyed the positioning of a torch to show a jagged hand, the gradual darkening of the stage, the subtle movements of shadows, and the loud grunge, which made sense once you realise what the play is actually about. The soundscape in general was masterful – deep, energetic bursts of noise and underlying clawing melodies that lifted the tension and crescendoed at exactly the right moment. The set was very effective – a doll’s house letting us see into every room, lit beautifully, letting our eyes dart around and watch out for action.

This was an impressive production. We didn’t know the original film, and this didn’t matter, as the story stands alone. Overall, it left us with just the right level of disquiet and the sense of menace was real. Now on tour after a West End run, this shows just how versatile our theatre can be, rising to the challenge of portraying horror in a live theatre setting. You may want to leave the light on afterwards, but then again, you may want to turn it off and enjoy the darkness that surrounds us all.
